summary:
Travel documents are the sharpest risk for a trans visitor to the United States. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records.

Screening at US checkpoints carries an outing risk: TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy. Multiple foreign governments have responded. In April 2025 CNN reported that several countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules; Axios reported in March 2025 that at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the US.

Facilities access is restricted in a growing number of states. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states; 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban, and some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol in what civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.

State document rules are tightening. In February 2026 Kansas enacted a law preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences and invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth, and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups call it a template for other states, with further targeting bills pending in state legislatures. A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest "Do Not Travel" state for trans people, bringing the total to four states so flagged, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends.

Visa screening carries its own exposure. In February 2025 the State Department announced a ban on trans athletes entering the US to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent ban on grounds of fraud.

Federal custody presents documented harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication, and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In ICE custody, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced-labour programmes, with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting "radical gender ideology" and characterised as "domestic terrorist groups"; a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy stated that activities would prioritise the identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is "anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." Advocates have compared these actions to the early stages of genocide.

Care access is constrained for visitors needing it. Executive Order 14187 (January 2025) described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is already banned in 27 states. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.
tangentialFactors:
The federal posture differs from state practice in ways a visitor may notice at different points of a trip. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia impose no state-level ban on trans people using facilities consistent with their gender identity, while nine states and one territory restrict such use in schools and some government buildings; the practical environment therefore varies sharply by itinerary. Kansas's February 2026 law is described by rights groups as a template, and a July 2026 assessment flagged four states as "Do Not Travel" for trans people, suggesting the sub-national picture is moving in one direction rather than stabilising.

Foreign governments treat the United States as a changed destination. Advisories issued in early 2025 by multiple countries, and adjusted travel guidelines from at least eight European states, place the US in a category where allied governments formally warn their own trans citizens. That is unusual for a destination of comparable diplomatic standing and is a reasonable proxy for how seriously document and data rules are taken abroad.

Several federal measures remain contested in court. The passport sex-marker restrictions were allowed to proceed by the Supreme Court in November 2025, but the Wikipedia survey records that a number of the executive orders have been blocked or enjoined, and the ACLU suit on behalf of seven plaintiffs is pending. The legal position is therefore active rather than settled, and a visitor's experience may differ from a reading of any single order.
localsOnly:
State identity-document rules govern what a resident can hold, independent of federal passport policy. MAP's identity-document map sets out which states allow gender-marker changes on a driver's licence or birth certificate and under what conditions; Kansas has closed both routes as of February 2026 and invalidated existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth.

Executive Order 14168 also reaches federal workplaces: it rescinded policies requiring use of names and pronouns consistent with a person's gender identity in federal workplaces, and mandated that federal agencies use "sex" rather than "gender" and remove materials that "promote gender ideology." A January 2025 list of "forbidden terms" circulated within government health-related agencies instructed employees to avoid words including "gender," "transgender" and "LGBT," and such words were removed from federal agency websites including the National Park Service Stonewall National Monument site; scientific grants mentioning LGBT topics were revoked.

Education and sport carry criminal and administrative exposure for residents. Executive Order 14190 (29 January 2025) directs law enforcement to investigate schools for promoting "gender ideology" and to criminally prosecute teachers who facilitate a transgender minor's social transition, including using preferred names or pronouns, potentially as sexual exploitation of a minor or practising medicine without a licence, with federal funding revoked for violating schools. Executive Order 14201 (5 February 2025), "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports," underpins the visa marking described above. An October 2025 rule blocks student loan forgiveness for public workers providing gender-affirming care to transgender youth, and an August 2025 threat to pull federal funding from sex education programmes mentioning transgender people led 11 states and two territories to comply by November 2025.

Residents in custody face the Federal Bureau of Prisons and ICE policies described above, and the Bureau of Prisons no longer publishes the count of transgender prisoners it holds. Residents under 18 seeking care face bans in 27 states and the proposed Medicaid exclusion; adults' access is not addressed by these particular measures.
outOfScopeNotes:
The scope of Executive Order 14168's facilities clause as applied to a foreign visitor in privately operated venues is not resolved in the sources; the order bars access to government-funded single-sex facilities, and the practical reach in hotels, restaurants and retail is not stated.

Whether a foreign visitor's own national passport carrying an X marker or a marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth will be accepted for entry, or will trigger secondary screening, is not directly addressed in the inventory. The sources document US-issued passport policy and foreign travel advisories, not port-of-entry treatment of third-country documents.

The "SWS25" visa marking and the fraud-based permanent ban are reported in connection with the sports-related State Department announcement of February 2025; whether the marking or the fraud finding extends to non-athlete visa categories is not stated in the sources.

The Queer Compass guide's advice to check recent violence reports before travel is a general instruction; the inventory contains no consolidated national figure for anti-trans hate crimes or their year-on-year direction, so the level of street violence risk is not sourced here.

Several federal measures are recorded as blocked or enjoined in court without a per-order status table; which specific orders remain in force as of the latest source date is not resolved in this inventory.
